source.title: Scaling Interpretable Transformers with Parity Bottleneck Layers
source.authors: Andrew Mack; K. Tou; Mark C. Henry; Zheng-Xun Wu; Lauren Greenspan

page_placements.theme: SAE width, sparsity, architecture, regularizers and supervision change latent monosemanticity

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper takes superposition and feature interpretability as motivation for its architecture, but it does not measure neuron polysemanticity or test whether neurons have coherent jobs.
record.gate_note: The paper reports interpretability metrics and interventions on bottleneck/SAE features, not measurements of neuron responses to unrelated inputs. The signed-activation observation and feature-absorption benchmark are related to feature interpretability but do not directly test any listed claim version. Causal-editing and steering results assess controllability, not polysemanticity.
record.test_reason: The paper introduces a sparse bottleneck architecture (ParityTransformer), motivated by superposition. It reports only its own method's interpretability and capability metrics against post-hoc SAEs. It never measures whether MLP neurons, or vision neurons, respond to unrelated inputs, how often they do, or what causes it. The variance auxiliary loss mentions 'low-variance polysemantic features' but gives no count or rate.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that parity bottlenecks make sparse features native to the forward pass at GPT-2 scale, at an 'interpretability tax' of 5-10x tokens and 1.2-2.1x throughput. They report matching or beating post-hoc SAEs on sparse probing, absorption, steering and causal edits, while trailing them on AutoInterp.
record.recipe_differences: The paper introduces and evaluates a parity-hash bottleneck architecture; it does not reproduce the original neuron visualization or SoLU method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that positive and negative activations for the same feature index often correspond to unrelated concepts, motivating sign-unfolding. Its steering results also use different steering strategies for DPB and SAE features, but those results do not test the listed versions.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report that positive and negative activations of the same bottleneck feature index mostly correspond to semantically unrelated concepts. They therefore split each index into two sign-specific features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In sign-symmetric (AbsTopK) sparse bottlenecks, opposite activation signs of one feature index typically encode unrelated concepts.

fits_no_version.finding: At layer 12, SAEBench absorption is 0.01 for the Parity Bottleneck, versus 0.807 for a TopK SAE and 0.180 for a Matryoshka SAE. The Parity Bottleneck trails both on AutoInterp (0.796 vs 0.859/0.891).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-loop sparse bottleneck features show less feature absorption than post-hoc SAE features, but lower auto-interpretability scores.

record.problems: The paper does not quantify polysemanticity or identify and test individual neurons. The signed-activation observation is qualitative and does not specify the model checkpoint or a measurement procedure. The feature-absorption values are reported without uncertainty estimates in Table 4.
record.rows_left_out: Causal feature-editing and steering results (Figure 2 and Figure 3) are omitted because they measure controllability and fluency/concept injection, not neuron mixed selectivity or polysemanticity. Other SAEBench metrics are likewise not direct measurements of the listed versions.

untested.parts: No vision models or image-classifier neurons.
No share of polysemantic MLP neurons in language models is measured, at any layer.
Superposition is cited as motivation only; capacity pressure is not tested as a cause of polysemantic neurons.
Initialization, regularization and training noise are not examined as causes.
The architecture changes the representation at a capability and data cost (6.7-9.4x tokens). It does not measure the share of polysemantic neurons before and after the change.
No reanalysis of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No comparison of activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods for classifying neurons. The sign-split of features is a related idea but is not tested on neurons.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T4 / uses_without_test assessment is confirmed. No verdicts are given because no row measures any version. The steering and causal-editing results are rightly left out: they measure controllability, not polysemanticity.

versions.untested_parts: No vision models or image-classifier neurons are examined.
No share of polysemantic MLP neurons in language models is measured.
The paper discusses superposition as motivation but does not test whether capacity pressure causes neuron polysemanticity.
Initialization, regularization, and training noise are not tested as causes of neuron polysemanticity.
The paper compares bottleneck features and post-hoc SAEs, but does not measure the share of polysemantic neurons or test lowering that share against capability costs.
The paper does not investigate whether apparently mixed neuron responses share a coherent feature.
The paper does not compare ways of measuring neuron polysemanticity across activation ranges or explanation scores.

rows.subject: ParityTransformer models (specific checkpoint not stated)
rows.operation_detail: The authors report that positive and negative activations of the same feature index usually correspond to semantically unrelated concepts; they unfold each index into separate positive and negative features for downstream tasks.
rows.measure: Semantic relatedness of concepts associated with the two activation signs
rows.value: Most of the time, positive and negative activations for the same feature index correspond to semantically unrelated concepts.
rows.note: This is about opposite signs of a designed bottleneck feature, not one neuron responding to several unrelated inputs.
rows.check: Qualitative remark with no checkpoint, procedure or number. It concerns the opposite signs of a designed bottleneck feature index (L0 indices are residual-stream basis directions, L1+ are parity hashes), not MLP neurons. It bears on no version.

tranche.reason: The paper builds a sparse-bottleneck architecture motivated by superposition and reports only its own method's capability and interpretability metrics against SAEs. It never measures how polysemantic the neurons are.
